sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Tradescantia zebrina is a fast-growing trailing tropical perennial native from Mexico to Colombia, grown for green, silver and white stripes with purple leaf undersides. It roots readily at stem nodes.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Trailing, creeping stems carry two-ranked leaves with silver/white stripes and purple undersides; nodes are about an inch apart.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Filtered sun is ideal; gradual full-sun exposure may deepen colour, but strong southern sun can wash colour or scorch leaves.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water regularly, let the mix dry between waterings, and reduce watering in winter.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use moist but well-drained soil or potting mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State gives 65–75°F as the preferred range; protect from cold drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average home humidity is tolerated; higher humidity is also acceptable.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use a dilute balanced houseplant feed during active growth; reduce or pause in winter. The species page does not give a fertilizer dose.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Hard prune in spring if needed to control trailing growth and encourage denser foliage.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Use stem cuttings from pruned growth; stems root at the nodes.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State lists low-severity poison characteristics: ingestion may irritate the mouth or stomach, and sap or foliage contact can irritate skin. Keep from pets and children; wear gloves if sap-sensitive.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for aphids, mealybugs, scale, whiteflies and spider mites. Soggy mix can cause root or stem rot; wet crowded foliage can develop leaf spot.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, provide filtered light, check pots more often in hot dry weather, and keep containers draining freely during monsoon rains. This is a local practical adjustment to the source’s moisture guidance.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Tradescantia spathacea forms a stiff-leaved basal rosette, unlike the trailing T. zebrina. Care below uses NC State Tradescantia genus guidance; species-specific thresholds may differ.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Look for an upright rosette of sword-shaped leaves, often green above and purple below. The linked source is genus-level, so confirm against the plant label or a species account.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Start in bright filtered light. Tradescantia can tolerate sun, but harsh afternoon sun may scorch leaves.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water when the top inch of mix dries; aim for moist, not saturated, soil.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use humus-rich, acidic potting mix that drains freely.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Genus guidance places tropical Tradescantia near 60–80°F; protect this tropical species from cold drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average indoor humidity is usually workable; prioritize airflow and avoid keeping the rosette constantly wet.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use dilute balanced feed during active growth; pause when growth slows. No species-specific fertilizer rate is established.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead outer leaves and old flower stalks at their base; avoid cutting the central rosette.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide mature rosettes or root offsets; the source’s genus-level stem-cutting advice mainly suits trailing forms.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State assigns low-severity poison characteristics to the Tradescantia genus. Treat ingestion and sap exposure as potential irritants; keep away from children and pets until species-specific safety is known.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Avoid waterlogged mix and inspect for common houseplant pests; the linked source is genus-level and does not establish a species-specific pest list.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, shelter the rosette from harsh afternoon sun and ensure monsoon rain drains freely; this local seasonal advice is practical, not source-specific.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Syngonium podophyllum is a tropical shrub that becomes a climbing vine with age. NC State describes juvenile arrow-shaped foliage and mature leaves that become lobed or divided.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Juvenile Syngonium podophyllum leaves are arrow-shaped; mature leaves become lobed and may divide into several segments. Leaf shape changes with maturity, so assess age before judging identity.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide bright shade or partial shade. NC State cautions that full sun can burn or bleach Syngonium podophyllum foliage.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the Syngonium podophyllum growing medium moist; avoid leaving the roots saturated. The source does not give a fixed watering interval.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a fertile, well-drained houseplant mix; a moss pole supports its mature climbing habit.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm and humid, away from cold drafts; bright shade avoids sun scorch.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: NC State recommends a warm, humid setting for Syngonium podophyllum. Provide airflow and avoid stagnant, persistently wet foliage.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly during active growth; the NC State species page gives no precise rate.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: To keep juvenile arrowhead foliage and a bushier habit, cut stems back as they begin to climb. NC State also notes that trimming roots during occasional repotting can help manage size.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists division, layering and stem cuttings for Syngonium podophyllum.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: Syngonium podophyllum contains calcium oxalate crystals. NC State reports oral irritation and swelling, drooling, vomiting and difficulty swallowing after exposure; keep away from children and pets and avoid sap contact.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports aphids, mealybugs and spider mites, plus bacterial leaf spots and soft rot, on Syngonium podophyllum. Check for the cause before treatment.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Nephrolepis exaltata is a tropical/subtropical terrestrial or epiphytic fern grown as the Boston fern houseplant. It produces arching fronds and spores on the undersides.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Nephrolepis exaltata is a Boston fern with divided fronds bearing rows of leaflets; spores form on the undersides of mature fronds. The ASPCA toxicity entry is specifically for the Boston fern form.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Give Boston fern bright, indirect light.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep Boston fern soil moist and do not let it dry out completely. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows, while avoiding waterlogged roots.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use rich, moist fern mix with good drainage; do not let the Boston fern root ball dry completely.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State gives 60–70°F (about 16–21°C) as a suitable warm indoor range for Nephrolepis exaltata.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Boston fern needs high humidity. A humid room or pebble tray can help; allow air movement around the fronds.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed with diluted liquid fertilizer during active growth; reduce watering as it slows in winter.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead fronds at the base. Brown sori underneath are normal spores, not pests.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide established clumps or grow from spores; division is the simpler home method.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Dry air can bring scale and spider mites; also watch for fern caterpillars. Brown sori on fronds are normal.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Maintain moisture and humidity in warm weather; reduce watering during the winter slowdown without letting the root ball dry.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Asplenium nidus is a tropical evergreen epiphytic fern. Its upright, strap-shaped fronds form a funnel-shaped rosette that catches leaf litter.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Look for broad, simple, strap-shaped fronds with wavy margins and a dark midrib, arranged in a central funnel-shaped rosette. Asplenium nidus reproduces by spores rather than flowers or fruit.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light or light shade suits Asplenium nidus; excess sun may yellow the fronds or slow growth.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the porous fern medium moist and do not allow Asplenium nidus to dry out. Use an open mix so moisture does not become waterlogging.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a rich, moist, porous fern mix for this epiphyte.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State says Asplenium nidus will not survive below 40°F (about 4°C); its ideal temperature range is 60–70°F (about 16–21°C).

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: This rainforest fern does not tolerate dry conditions; provide high humidity while avoiding stagnant air.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: NC State notes that active growth may benefit from a monthly application of dilute liquid fertilizer. Use a conservative dilution and reduce feeding when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove damaged fronds at their base; avoid cutting the central growing point.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Propagate from spores; do not split a single crown. Keep young plants warm and humid.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Asplenium nidus is susceptible to slugs, snails, scale, mealybugs, bacterial leaf diseases and leaf nematodes. NC State cautions that the fronds are fragile and sensitive to chemical insecticides.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Keep warm, frost-free and away from drafts; NC State notes this species can be damaged below 40°F.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Phlebodium aureum is a rhizomatous epiphytic fern from the American tropics. Its creeping golden-scaled rhizomes and deeply lobed blue-green fronds distinguish it from true palms despite the common name cabbage palm fern.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Identify Phlebodium aureum by its creeping, golden-scaled rhizomes and large, deeply lobed fronds; round sori occur in rows on either side of the pinna midrib.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide partial shade or dappled light for Phlebodium aureum.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Use a moist but not soggy substrate. Phlebodium aureum tolerates some drying between waterings.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a loose, organic, acidic medium with good drainage for this epiphytic fern.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm and away from cold drafts; avoid hard temperature swings.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Medium to high humidity and good air circulation suit Phlebodium aureum. Frond browning can indicate low humidity; curling can signal low humidity or underwatering.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly with dilute balanced fertilizer during active growth; reduce when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead fronds only and leave creeping golden-scaled rhizomes exposed.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide the creeping rhizome with a growing point attached; use airy organic medium.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State lists spider mites, thrips, fern caterpillars and fungus gnats, with crown or root rot as possible diseases for Phlebodium aureum.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from harsh afternoon sun and monsoon saturation; keep substrate moist, not soggy.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Adiantum raddianum (Delta maidenhair) is a delicate clumping fern with arching, finely divided fronds and creeping rhizomes. NC State gives it partial shade, moist soil and humid indoor conditions.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Flat, finely divided fronds have triangular lobed pinnules on shiny wiry black stems. This is the Delta maidenhair, not a generic Adiantum identification.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide partial shade to shade; too much shade weakens growth and full sun damages this fern.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep soil moist to wet and do not let the roots dry out; drain excess standing water.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a moist, organic, well-drained fern mix; keep the creeping rhizomes near the surface.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Typical warm indoor temperatures are suitable; avoid cold drafts. A genus-level K-State guide gives 60–70°F as a useful indoor range.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: High humidity helps indoors; K-State suggests a humid room or terrarium and warns that extra watering cannot compensate for dry air.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed cautiously at about one-quarter label strength every 4–6 weeks during active growth; do not feed when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove discolored or dead fronds; K-State notes older fronds naturally die after several months.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide a healthy clump in spring, keeping rhizome and roots intact.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports few significant pests or diseases, but fern caterpillar can occur. Sudden wet/dry swings and low humidity commonly stress indoor maidenhair ferns.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from direct afternoon sun and keep evenly moist in hot weather; reduce watering only if growth slows, never allowing the root ball to dry.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Platycerium bifurcatum is an epiphytic staghorn fern that grows on support rather than parasitizing a host. It forms sterile shield fronds and branching fertile fronds.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Staghorn fern has two frond forms: flat shield fronds at the base and branching, antler-like fertile fronds bearing sori.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide dappled light to partial shade for Platycerium bifurcatum.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water the crown regularly, allowing roots to dry slightly between waterings but not to dry out completely. Ensure drainage.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: For a pot-grown Platycerium bifurcatum, use an epiphytic orchid mix or sphagnum moss; it can also be mounted on wood or bark.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Grow warm; this tropical epiphyte is suited to frost-free conditions.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Provide humid air with good airflow; black spot may occur if humidity is excessive and air stagnant.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Allow shield fronds to trap leaf litter as natural nutrients; use only dilute feed if growth is weak.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Keep the brown shield fronds in place; remove only dead fertile fronds.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: The fern forms pups from rhizomes. NC State notes that large colonies can be divided.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for spider mites, aphids and mealybugs. NC State notes black spot may occur when humidity is too high.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Shade from harsh Dhaka afternoon sun and protect from prolonged monsoon saturation; water crown while roots dry slightly.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Asparagus densiflorus is not a true fern: it is an arching, fern-like member of Asparagaceae. NC State describes its red berries and indoor growth habit.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Asparagus densiflorus has scale-like true leaves and flattened, needle-like cladodes in clusters; red berries may form.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: NC State notes that Asparagus densiflorus tolerates shade and that afternoon sun in warmer climates may yellow foliage.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: NC State describes regular watering from spring through autumn and sparing watering in winter for Asparagus densiflorus; it does not tolerate wet soils.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a well-drained mix; this asparagus fern is intolerant of wet soil.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep frost-free; bring container plants indoors before cold nights.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average indoor humidity is acceptable; prioritize drainage and airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use dilute balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth; reduce or pause in slow periods.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Pinch stem tips to maintain height and encourage a denser Asparagus densiflorus form; NC State notes it can be cut to soil level to regenerate.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide the fleshy root crown or grow from seed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Inspect for mites, aphids, mealybugs, leaf spot and root/crown rot; afternoon sun may yellow foliage.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Asparagus setaceus is not a true fern; its fine, feathery foliage belongs to the asparagus family (Asparagaceae). NC State reports a native range from Ethiopia to South Africa.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Asparagus setaceus has delicate, feathery branchlets and small scale-like leaves; it may produce berries. The common name fern describes appearance, not taxonomy.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light; this species is intolerant of high light intensity.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water regularly from spring to autumn and sparingly in winter.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use slightly acidic, organic-rich, moist but well-drained potting mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State gives 55–70°F as its preferred range; keep frost-free.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: High humidity helps prevent yellowing and needle drop; a humidifier or pebble tray can help.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use dilute balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth; reduce or pause in slow periods.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Cut damaged or overgrown stems to the root rather than shortening them halfway; tip-pinch for shape.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Propagate by division or seed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State reports that Asparagus setaceus berries can cause abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea if eaten, and sap may irritate skin. Keep berries away from children and pets; wear gloves when pruning.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Yellow needles and leaf drop follow insufficient light or water; watch for pests and root/crown rot.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.content: A compact, spreading nerve plant with prominent contrasting leaf veins; high humidity and evenly moist, well-drained medium are important.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Oval leaves with conspicuous red, pink or white netted veins; leaf colour varies by cultivar.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: RHS recommends filtered light for Fittonia; protect leaves from harsh direct sun. This is species-level guidance shared by the two catalog names.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the Fittonia growing medium moist but well drained; avoid letting the root ball dry completely or remain waterlogged.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a moisture-retentive but well-drained growing medium for Fittonia.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep above 17°C (63°F) and away from cold drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: RHS identifies high humidity as beneficial for Fittonia. Maintain airflow and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use dilute balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth; reduce or pause in slow periods.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Pinch leggy stems and remove yellow leaves with clean tools; avoid heavy pruning at once.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Stem cuttings or division may work depending on the species; use clean tools and airy, lightly moist medium.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Pilea peperomioides is a compact, clumping evergreen houseplant native to Yunnan, China. Its round peltate leaves attach to long petioles at the center of each blade.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: The round, fleshy leaves of Pilea peperomioides are peltate: each long petiole attaches near the centre of the blade. Houseplants rarely flower.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Give Pilea peperomioides bright indirect light.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Use a moist but well-drained potting mix for Pilea peperomioides; avoid leaving it saturated.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use moist, well-drained potting mix in a pot with drainage.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Avoid cold drafts and direct heat sources.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Moderate to high humidity is fine; average indoor humidity is tolerated.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly during active spring/summer growth; no dose is specified by NC State.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove yellow leaves and rotate the pot for balanced growth; protect the central crown.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Separate pups or root stem cuttings in spring or early summer.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for spider mites, mealybugs, fungus gnats and scale. Overwatering causes root rot; low light causes legginess.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Aspidistra elatior is an evergreen, rhizomatous foliage plant with upright, leathery leaves; NC State describes it as a shade-tolerant groundcover and houseplant.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Aspidistra elatior grows hosta-like leathery leaves with parallel veins from rhizomes.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Aspidistra elatior prefers partial to full shade and is intolerant of direct sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water regularly in spring to autumn; during winter and drought water sparingly.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Rich, well-drained soil is preferred, though the species tolerates poorer soils.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Shelter from cold winter winds; avoid frost in pots.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: No high-humidity requirement is noted; typical indoor air is tolerated.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed modestly during active growth; avoid heavy doses.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove damaged leaves at soil level and keep healthy foliage.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide rhizomes, retaining roots and several leaves on each division.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Few serious pest problems are reported; direct sun can damage leaves.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Strelitzia reginae is a clumping tropical perennial native to South Africa, grown for its bird-head-shaped orange and blue flower. Large gray-green leaves arise from underground rhizomes.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Strelitzia reginae has large gray-green leaves and an orange-and-blue flower emerging from a boat-shaped spathe. The flowers may appear intermittently through the year.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow Strelitzia reginae in a well-lit sunny position; outdoors it tolerates sun to partial shade with air circulation.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water Strelitzia reginae freely during active growth and keep it drier in winter; provide a well-drained medium.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use fertile loamy soil that drains well for Strelitzia reginae.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State suggests moderate temperatures with nights around 55–65°F; provide airflow in warm weather.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Normal room humidity with good airflow is adequate.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: NC State recommends regular fertilizing in spring and summer for Strelitzia reginae; reduce feeding during the drier winter rest.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove spent flower stalks and damaged leaves at the base.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists division for Strelitzia reginae.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State reports that Strelitzia reginae is toxic to cats, dogs and horses; it lists mild nausea, vomiting and drowsiness, mainly associated with fruit and seeds. Keep those parts away from animals.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Monitor Strelitzia reginae for mealybugs, scale and spider mites. Root rot can follow overwatering or poorly drained soil; leaf spot may cause yellow or brown marks.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, provide ventilation in hot weather and prevent monsoon waterlogging; water less during cooler, slower growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Dypsis lutescens (areca/butterfly palm) forms clumps of yellow-green canes with arching pinnate fronds. UF/IFAS recommends fertile, acidic, well-drained soil.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Identify by multiple golden-yellow cane-like stems and arching feather-shaped fronds; stem color may be less vivid in lower light.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright filtered light indoors; acclimate gradually to outdoor sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the root zone evenly moist in active growth but drain freely.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: UF/IFAS prefers fertile, acidic, well-drained soil for Dypsis lutescens.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm and avoid extended exposure to cool nights or cold drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Moderate to higher humidity helps indoors; inspect for spider mites in dry rooms.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use palm or balanced fertilizer at label rate in active growth; avoid repeated heavy feeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove only fully dead or damaged fronds; never cut the central growing point.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Grow from seed or separate well-rooted basal clumps; avoid splitting a single stem.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: ASPCA lists Dypsis lutescens (areca palm) as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses. This is a pet-specific listing, not a human-safety assessment.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Check for spider mites, scale and leaf-tip browning; assess light, water and salt buildup.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, ensure monsoon rain drains freely and acclimate to sun; water less in cooler, slower growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Chamaedorea elegans is a solitary-stemmed understory palm from southern Mexico and Central America, commonly sold as several seedlings together in one pot.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Slender cane-like stems carry pinnate fronds of narrow leaflets. Several stems in one pot are usually separate seedlings rather than a clumping plant.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light is preferred, though this palm tolerates lower light.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Let the mix dry slightly between waterings; it grows lushly with steady moisture but must not sit in water.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use humus-rich, well-drained houseplant mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Protect from cold drafts near windows, doors and vents.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Low to medium humidity is tolerated.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed periodically during the growing season; stop in winter.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove only fully dead or damaged fronds; never cut the central growing point.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Chamaedorea elegans is solitary-stemmed and usually grown from seed; do not divide its crown.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State describes this palm as not hazardous for pets, but says fruit pulp can irritate sensitive skin. This is not a human ingestion assessment; prevent children and pets from eating plant material.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Avoid overwatering and inspect for scale or spider mites. Fruit pulp can irritate sensitive skin.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, ensure monsoon rain drains freely and acclimate to sun; water less in cooler, slower growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Rhapis excelsa is the lady palm, a fan-leaved palm grown in clumps. NC State notes that interior specimens rarely flower.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Rhapis excelsa forms clumps on underground rhizomes; its fan-shaped leaves are usually divided into five to seven segments with blunt, shredded-looking tips.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Indirect light is best; Rhapis excelsa tolerates deep shade indoors.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water regularly but drain freely; reduce watering in winter.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use well-drained potting soil.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Bring outdoors-grown pots inside before temperatures fall below 50°F.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Low humidity is tolerated.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply balanced slow-release fertilizer during active growth.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove only dead fronds; do not cut healthy green foliage or the growing point.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide rooted shoots from the rhizome.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Check for mites, mealybugs, scale and occasional leaf spot.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, ensure monsoon rain drains freely and acclimate to sun; water less in cooler, slower growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Ravenea rivularis (majesty palm) is a large tropical evergreen palm often sold as a container houseplant. UF/IFAS recommends bright indirect light, warmth, humidity and moist, well-drained soil.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: The catalog label is Ravenea rivularis (majesty palm). Compare the plant’s trunk and arching pinnate crown with a mature species reference; young palms can be hard to identify from foliage alone.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light; direct sun can scorch the leaves.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep soil moist but well-drained; avoid a pot standing in water.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a well-drained loam or container mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm, away from cold drafts or direct heat.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: This palm prefers high humidity; maintain airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use palm or balanced fertilizer at label rate in active growth; avoid repeated heavy feeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead fronds at the base; do not cut the central growing point.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Grow from seed; do not divide a single-stem crown.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: UF/IFAS reports no serious pest or disease problems; check for root rot if soil remains wet.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, ensure monsoon rain drains freely and acclimate to sun; water less in cooler, slower growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Beaucarnea recurvata is an evergreen, drought-tolerant succulent tree native to Mexico. The swollen caudex stores water; the common name ponytail palm is misleading because it is not a true palm.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Look for a swollen water-storing caudex and long, narrow, curling leaves. Beaucarnea recurvata is in the asparagus family, not the palm family.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide a sunny window for Beaucarnea recurvata; acclimate gradually before moving it to a protected patio.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water deeply in summer, then let the mix dry between waterings. Greatly reduce watering in winter.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a cactus/succulent mix with good drainage for Beaucarnea recurvata.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State describes Beaucarnea recurvata as hardy to about 50°F (10°C); bring container plants into protection before colder conditions.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Ordinary indoor humidity is suitable; ponytail palm tolerates dry air.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly during active growth; do not feed during its dry winter rest.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead leaf tips or lower leaves with clean scissors; do not cut into the swollen caudex.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Seed is typical; separate basal offsets only when they have their own roots.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Houseplants may develop mealybugs, scale or spider mites; NC State also lists stem rot, bacterial leaf streak and leaf spots.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give bright light and monsoon rain shelter; let mix dry well, especially in cooler months.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Tropical hibiscus is an evergreen flowering shrub with glossy foliage and large short-lived flowers; cultivar characteristics vary.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Glossy evergreen leaves and large showy flowers; flower colour, form and size vary widely among cultivars.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Smithsonian Gardens recommends a bright position for tropical Hibiscus rosa-sinensis; provide strong light and acclimate container plants to direct sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the root zone of tropical Hibiscus rosa-sinensis moist, with good drainage. Avoid leaving container roots in standing water.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use rich, moist soil with good drainage for Hibiscus rosa-sinensis.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis is a tender tropical shrub; protect it from frost and cold wind. NC State lists outdoor hardiness zones 9–11.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: NC State notes that Hibiscus rosa-sinensis appreciates high humidity; maintain airflow around container-grown plants.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply balanced fertilizer during active growth and flowering; avoid a concentrated dose on dry roots.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: For Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, prune to shape during active growth; it flowers on new growth. Avoid severe pruning when a near-term display is wanted.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists stem cuttings for Hibiscus rosa-sinensis.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports no major problems for Hibiscus rosa-sinensis but recommends watching for scale insects.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Protect from cold and wind; prune in early spring because hibiscus flowers on new growth. In Dhaka, shelter pots from monsoon saturation.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Ixora coccinea is a compact tropical evergreen shrub native to Bangladesh and neighbouring South and Southeast Asian regions. It bears red tubular flower clusters and grows about 4–6 ft tall in the cited landscape account.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Ixora coccinea has leathery opposite leaves and red tubular four-petaled flowers clustered at branch ends; dark purple to black drupes follow flowering.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Full sun supports flowering in Ixora coccinea; it tolerates a small amount of afternoon shade.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the root zone moist but well drained. NC State describes Ixora coccinea as preferring moist soil; avoid waterlogging containers.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use organically rich, acidic, well-drained soil for Ixora coccinea. Alkaline soil can cause chlorosis.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State says Ixora coccinea is intolerant of temperatures below 50°F (10°C); protect container plants from cool conditions.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm humid conditions suit this tropical shrub; ensure airflow through the canopy.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly during active growth; do not overfertilize or allow alkaline soil to induce chlorosis.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: NC State recommends pruning Ixora coccinea in late winter when shaping is needed.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists stem cuttings for Ixora coccinea.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Ixora coccinea may be affected by aphids, thrips, scale, bagworms, nematodes and mealybugs; sooty mold and mushroom root rot are also reported. Alkaline soil can cause chlorosis.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Protect from temperatures below 50°F. In Dhaka, provide morning sun and free drainage during monsoon rains.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Dwarf ixora is a compact selection of Ixora coccinea. NC State supports the parent species’ tropical shrub culture, but the exact dwarf cultivar and its mature size are unknown.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Ixora coccinea has leathery dark-green leaves and clusters of tubular flowers; the dwarf selection’s exact cultivar traits are unconfirmed.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: The parent species flowers best in full sun and tolerates a little afternoon shade.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the root zone evenly moist during active growth, but do not leave the pot saturated.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use organically rich, acidic, well-drained soil; alkaline mix can cause chlorosis.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Ixora coccinea is tender below about 50°F; keep the dwarf container warm.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm tropical humidity suits Ixora; space plants for airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer during active growth; avoid high pH and overfeeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: The parent species is best pruned in late winter; prune lightly to preserve the dwarf habit.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: The species is propagated by stem cuttings; named dwarf cultivars may not come true from seed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: No species-specific toxicity assessment for this dwarf selection is provided here. As a precaution, do not ingest it and keep it away from children and pets.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for aphids, thrips, scale, mealybugs, sooty mold and mushroom root rot; alkaline soil may cause chlorosis.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Protect this tropical shrub from cool spells and keep container drainage open through Dhaka monsoon rain.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Gardenia jasminoides is an evergreen shrub native to southern China and Japan, known for fragrant white flowers and glossy dark-green foliage.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Gardenia jasminoides has glossy, dark-green opposite or whorled leaves and fragrant white flowers that age cream or yellow. Its pinwheel-like buds are a useful cue.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Gardenia jasminoides prefers bright indirect light or partial shade; shelter it from strong wind and cold exposure.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Gardenia jasminoides is moderately drought tolerant once established. Keep container soil evenly moist but well drained; do not let the pot stand in water.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use rich, acidic, well-drained soil for Gardenia jasminoides. Avoid root disturbance because its roots are shallow.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Protect from cold and strong winds; cold exposure can cause winter burn.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Gardenia tolerates outdoor humidity; maintain airflow and avoid crowding.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Do not fertilize in fall; use an acid-forming fertilizer during active spring growth if needed.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune Gardenia jasminoides in spring to shape; it flowers on new growth. Removing spent flowers can encourage further bloom.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists grafting, layering, seed and stem cuttings for Gardenia jasminoides.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State lists low-severity toxicity for Gardenia jasminoides and reports mild vomiting or diarrhea and hives. Keep ingestion risk in mind around children and pets.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State notes whiteflies can affect stressed Gardenia jasminoides; alkaline soil near concrete may also impair growth.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Prune and shape in spring, then remove spent flowers; avoid root disturbance and keep soil acidic.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Jasminum sambac is Arabian jasmine, a tropical shrub or vine with fragrant flowers. NC State’s linked guide is for Jasminum as a genus, so use the care below as a starting point rather than a species-specific prescription.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Use the botanical name Jasminum sambac as the catalog identification. Detailed diagnostic traits and cultivar distinctions require a species-specific source review.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: The Jasminum genus guide recommends full sun or at least bright light; acclimate a container plant gradually.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Most jasmines prefer moist, well-drained soil, although some species tolerate drier conditions.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use moist, well-drained potting mix; the linked advice is genus-level.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep this tropical jasmine warm and shelter from cold drafts; no exact temperature threshold was found in the linked source.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Normal warm outdoor humidity is acceptable; provide airflow around a dense shrub.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed modestly during active growth; no species-specific fertilizer rate is stated in the genus source.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune after flowering, as jasmine flowers form on older growth; avoid trimming before the bloom flush.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Use stem cuttings or layering as practical options for a woody jasmine; species response can vary.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: No species-specific toxicity evaluation is included here. Do not ingest it or use it medicinally; keep away from children and pets until checked.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: The genus guide notes aphids, spider mites, leaf spot and root rot; outdoor pest problems are often uncommon.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Grow warm, provide bright light and prune after the main flowering period; Dhaka rain and heat adjustments are practical rather than directly sourced.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Trachelospermum jasminoides (star jasmine) is an evergreen twining vine native to Japan and China. Despite its common name and fragrant flowers, it is not in the genus Jasminum.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Star jasmine has opposite glossy leaves and fragrant, creamy-white pinwheel flowers. Milky latex appears from cut or bruised stems.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: For best flowering, grow Trachelospermum jasminoides in a sunny sheltered position; NC State also lists partial shade tolerance.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Once established, Trachelospermum jasminoides is drought tolerant. Water container plants according to root-zone moisture and maintain drainage.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use fertile, well-drained soil for Trachelospermum jasminoides.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Shelter from cold; in colder climates grow in a container and overwinter indoors.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Normal outdoor humidity is suitable; prioritize a sunny, sheltered position and airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply spring fertilizer only if the soil is not fertile.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune Trachelospermum jasminoides after flowering to keep it within its support or container. Clean tools after contact with sticky milky sap.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists stem cuttings and layering for Trachelospermum jasminoides.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports few serious pest or disease problems for Trachelospermum jasminoides; Japanese beetles may occur.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Give support as the vine grows; after the late-spring flowering, prune to fit its space.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Adenium obesum is a drought-tolerant succulent shrub with a swollen caudex, native to Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. NC State reports a slow growth rate and summer flowering.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Adenium obesum has a thick gray-green caudex, glossy leaves near branch tips, showy five-lobed flowers and paired pod-like follicles. Flower colours and forms vary among cultivars.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow Adenium obesum in full sun; acclimate a sheltered container plant gradually when moving it outdoors.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Let the succulent growing medium dry between waterings. Water during active growth; reduce watering during dormancy. Excessively wet soil can cause rot.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a cactus/succulent medium and a pot with multiple drainage holes. NC State specifies good drainage for Adenium obesum.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Bring indoors when outdoor temperatures approach 55°F; avoid cold, wet roots.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average indoor humidity is acceptable; dry air is less harmful than wet soil.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply fertilizer in spring to support flowering.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune to shape during active warm growth; let cut surfaces dry before watering.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists seed, stem cuttings and grafting for Adenium obesum; success and retention of cultivar traits vary by method.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State reports cardiac glycosides and poisonous plant parts throughout Adenium obesum; ingestion can cause gastrointestinal and cardiac effects, and milky sap may cause contact dermatitis. Wear gloves when pruning and keep the plant away from children and pets.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State notes that persistently wet soil can cause rot; aphids, scale, mealybugs and occasional fungal leaf spot are reported. Confirm the cause before treatment.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Water during active growth and reduce watering while dormant; protect from cold and monsoon saturation.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Pentas lanceolata is a tropical flowering subshrub grown as a perennial in warm climates and as an annual or houseplant elsewhere. NC State describes clusters of star-shaped flowers from spring into fall.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Pentas lanceolata bears clusters of five-part, star-shaped flowers and lance-shaped foliage.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Pentas lanceolata flowers best in full sun, though it tolerates some shade.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water consistently while growing, allowing the soil surface to dry between waterings; pentas has moderate drought tolerance.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use organically rich, well-drained soil for Pentas lanceolata.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A tropical perennial in zones 10–11; elsewhere it is grown as an annual or houseplant.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm, humid conditions are suitable; indoor pentas benefits from airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use balanced flowering-plant fertilizer during active growth; reduce in slow periods.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove faded flower clusters and pinch leggy shoots to maintain a compact flowering form.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Sow seed in a warm location; NC State recommends starting indoors before the cool season ends.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Spider mites, aphids and leaf-chewing caterpillars may occur.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give morning sun and afternoon shade in peak heat; protect pots from monsoon waterlogging.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Catharanthus roseus (Madagascar periwinkle) is a tender, spreading evergreen perennial native to Madagascar, commonly grown as a bedding annual outside warm climates. NC State reports flowering through summer until frost.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Catharanthus roseus has glossy opposite leaves with a pale midrib and five-lobed salverform flowers, often with a contrasting eye; paired slender follicles form after flowering.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: NC State lists full sun through partial or dappled shade for Catharanthus roseus. In hot container settings, acclimate gradually and monitor wilting.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep moist but well-drained while establishing; once established, this species tolerates heat and some drought.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a well-drained medium; NC State notes the species prefers acidic soil but tolerates a range of soils when drainage is good.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A tender perennial in zones 10+; protect from frost or grow seasonally in cooler conditions.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: No special humidity treatment is needed outdoors; good drainage is more important in humid weather.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use modest balanced feeding; avoid excessive nitrogen that promotes leaves over flowers.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Modern compact hybrids generally need no pinching or deadheading; trim only damaged or sprawling growth.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists seed propagation for Catharanthus roseus. Cultivar-specific seed fidelity is not established by this source.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State identifies vinca alkaloids and reports that ingestion of large quantities of Catharanthus roseus can cause serious systemic effects. The source lists flowers, fruit, leaves, roots, seeds and stems as poisonous parts. Keep away from children and pets; do not use medicinally.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Avoid wet, poorly drained soil to reduce root and stem rots; inspect for leaf spot.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give morning sun and afternoon shade in peak heat; protect pots from monsoon waterlogging.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: African marigold (Tagetes erecta) is a warm-season annual. NC State’s Tagetes genus guide includes these species and gives broad care guidance; cultivar size and flower form vary.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: African marigold (Tagetes erecta) has aromatic, divided foliage and showy flower heads; often has larger flower heads, but cultivar forms vary.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Tagetes grows in full or partial sun; full sun usually encourages the best bloom.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water young plants as they establish; later, allow the soil to drain and avoid prolonged saturation. Some marigolds tolerate dry spells.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: A range of soil types is tolerated if drainage is good.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Grow as a warm-season annual; protect from prolonged cool weather.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Provide spacing and airflow during humid weather to reduce leaf and stem disease.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use moderate fertility; no species-specific fertilizer rate is given by the genus guide.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Deadhead faded flower heads for repeat bloom; leave some seed heads only if collecting seed.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Grow from seed; remove unwanted seed heads to limit reseeding.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State warns that large amounts may be harmful and that sap or contact can irritate skin. This is genus-level guidance; avoid ingestion and wear gloves if sensitive.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for spider mites, Japanese beetles and slugs; diseases can include wilt, stem rot, leaf spots, botrytis and aster yellows.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Grow in the cooler dry season in Dhaka where possible; protect containers from monsoon waterlogging and remove storm-damaged stems.

sections.title: Soil and drainage

sections.title: Temperature
