sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Zinnia elegans is an annual bedding and cut flower; NC State describes multiple flower forms, from single to double, in a wide range of colours.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Zinnia elegans is an erect annual with opposite, clasping leaves and large flower heads; cultivar colour and flower form vary.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Plant Zinnia elegans in full sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water at the soil line and allow good drainage; avoid keeping foliage wet.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Grow Zinnia elegans in loam or organic-rich soil with good drainage.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Zinnias flower through summer and fall but may slow at peak heat; choose disease-resistant varieties for hot, humid weather.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Good airflow and full sun help limit fungal leaf disease in humid conditions.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use moderately fertile soil; avoid heavy nitrogen that encourages leafy growth.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Deadhead if desired; continuous new blooms are cultivar-dependent.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Sow seed directly after cool weather has passed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Powdery mildew, leaf spots, root rots, blights, aphids, mites and Japanese beetles may occur.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Grow in the cooler dry season where possible; during monsoon use fast-draining pots and remove storm-damaged growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Cosmos bipinnatus is a tall, daisy-flowered annual native to Mexico or tropical America. NC State notes that it readily reseeds.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Cosmos bipinnatus produces daisy-like maroon, pink, lavender or white flowers on stems that may reach about 4 ft.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Give Cosmos bipinnatus at least a half-day of direct sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep seedbed moist for 5–10 days after sowing; afterward it needs only basic watering.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Sow into loose, ordinary garden soil; avoid burying seeds deeply.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Sow after cool weather has passed and soil is warm (about 65°F).

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Provide airflow through the finely divided foliage during humid weather.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Avoid rich, heavily fertilized soil; excess fertility can produce tall leafy growth with fewer flowers.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Deadhead to encourage further blooms; stake tall forms in windy or stormy conditions.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Sow seed shallowly outdoors after danger of frost; it readily reseeds.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for stem canker, powdery mildew and gray mold; aphids, leafhoppers and loopers may feed.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Grow in the cooler dry season where possible; during monsoon use fast-draining pots and remove storm-damaged growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Helianthus annuus is the common annual sunflower. NC State’s genus account includes H. annuus and supports full sun, moist soil and leaving stems/seed heads for wildlife; garden cultivar size varies.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Typical H. annuus has an erect stem, rough broad leaves and a large flower head with yellow rays around a central disc; branching and head size vary by cultivar.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow in full sun for the most blooms.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep soil reasonably moist in active growth; the genus includes species with different wet-soil tolerances.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Ordinary garden soil is suitable; soil moisture and drainage needs vary across Helianthus.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Grow annual sunflower in warm weather; sow when soil has warmed and protect young plants from storms.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Provide airflow and support tall stems during humid, stormy periods.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use ordinary fertile soil and avoid excessive nitrogen; no specific dose is given in the source.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Leave seed heads for birds. Cut dry stems to 12–24 inches and leave them standing for stem-nesting bees.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Grow annual H. annuus from seed; stake tall cultivars if exposed to wind.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: The cited genus source does not assess toxicity. Do not assume ornamental plant parts are safe to eat; keep away from children and pets pending a species-specific check.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Tall plants with large flower heads may need support; the NC State genus page reports no serious general pest or disease problems.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, use the cooler dry season for a better chance of flowering and stake tall cultivars before storms; this is local practical advice.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Celosia argentea is a tropical annual with several distinct flower forms, including plumed, finger-like and cockscomb types. Cultivar group determines the inflorescence shape.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Celosia argentea cultivars may have plume-shaped, finger-like or brain-like cockscomb inflorescences; identify the cultivar group before describing its flower form.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Celosia argentea prefers full sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Celosia argentea tolerates dry, porous soil and heat. Allow excess water to drain; crowded, wet conditions can rot flowers or roots.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use amended, well-drained soil for Celosia argentea; NC State notes tolerance of dry, porous soils.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Celosia thrives in heat and humidity; protect from cold.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: It tolerates heat and humidity, but crowding and persistent rain can rot flowers.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use modest feeding in well-amended soil; excessive nutrients are not needed for this heat-tolerant annual.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Deadhead if reseeding is unwanted; leave heads to mature if collecting seed.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Direct-sow or start seed indoors and transplant after cool weather has passed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Celosia argentea can develop root rot; snails and slugs may feed on it. High humidity, rain and crowding can cause flower rot; indoor plants may attract aphids and spider mites.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Grow in the cooler dry season where possible; during monsoon use fast-draining pots and remove storm-damaged growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Crossandra infundibuliformis is a tropical evergreen shrub or warm-season container plant with glossy, wavy-edged leaves and fan-shaped orange, salmon or related flowers. It prefers warm indoor air and high humidity.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Crossandra infundibuliformis has glossy opposite leaves with wavy edges and upright spikes bearing fan-shaped flowers with asymmetrical petals.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide bright indirect light; low light can stop flowering and direct sun can damage leaves.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Use warm water; cold water may shock roots. Keep mix lightly moist, not sodden.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use fertile, well-drained soil; for acid-loving types avoid lime and use an acid-forming mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm; temperatures below 55°F can cause leaf drop.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: High humidity supports flowering and propagation; use a pebble tray or humidifier without letting the pot stand in water.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply balanced fertilizer at label rate during active growth; avoid overfeeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Pinch after flowering; cut stems before seed pods form if you do not want explosive seed release.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Take early-season stem cuttings in seed-starting mix; warm humid conditions help rooting.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Check occasionally for mealybugs, whitefly, aphids and mites; heavy rain damages flowers.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, offer morning sun or filtered afternoon shade in peak heat and prevent prolonged monsoon saturation.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Tabernaemontana divaricata is an evergreen rounded tropical shrub with glossy lance-shaped leaves and waxy white pinwheel flowers. NParks lists sun to semi-shade, moderate water and moist but well-drained soil.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Compare the plant with Tabernaemontana divaricata: opposite glossy lance-shaped leaves, waxy white pinwheel flowers and milky sap when cut.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: NParks lists full sun to semi-shade for Tabernaemontana divaricata.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: NParks rates this species as moderate-water; keep the root zone moist but well drained.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: The species tolerates moist or well-drained root zones; avoid prolonged waterlogging in containers.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A tropical evergreen; protect potted plants from cold spells.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm tropical humidity is suitable; maintain airflow around the shrub.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply balanced fertilizer at label rate during active growth; avoid overfeeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune lightly to maintain shrub shape after flowering; avoid cutting more than needed.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Use stem cuttings or seed; keep cuttings warm and lightly moist while rooting.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: The NParks record does not list major pests; inspect for common shrub pests and remove affected growth.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, offer morning sun or filtered afternoon shade in peak heat and prevent prolonged monsoon saturation.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Chandni is listed as Tabernaemontana divaricata. NParks documents the species as an evergreen rounded shrub with white pinwheel flowers; the specific dwarf cultivar, if any, is not established by the catalog name.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Compare the plant with Tabernaemontana divaricata: opposite glossy lance-shaped leaves, white pinwheel flowers and milky sap when cut. The common name Chandni does not identify a cultivar by itself.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: The NParks dwarf form is listed for full sun to semi-shade.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: NParks lists moderate watering for the dwarf form; drain containers freely.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a moist but well-drained container mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep the dwarf tropical shrub warm and protect from cold drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm outdoor humidity suits this tropical shrub; give it airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Apply balanced fertilizer at label rate during active growth; avoid overfeeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Lightly shape after flowering; avoid severe cuts to an unidentified dwarf selection.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Use stem cuttings or seed as practical methods; cultivar fidelity is not guaranteed from seed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: No major problem list is supplied in the dwarf record; check periodically for scale, aphids and mites.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, offer morning sun or filtered afternoon shade in peak heat and prevent prolonged monsoon saturation.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: A fast-growing evergreen shrub with narrow leathery leaves and showy flowers. All parts are highly poisonous; do not ingest or burn.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Narrow linear-lanceolate leaves arranged opposite or in whorls; terminal clusters of five-lobed flowers.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Oleander grows in full sun to partial shade.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: NC State describes Nerium oleander as drought tolerant once established and adaptable to moist or occasionally dry, well-drained soils. For a container, water according to root-zone drying and prevent prolonged saturation.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use fertile, well-drained soil; it adapts to some soil variation.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Oleander can be damaged at or below 32°F; protect containers from cold.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: No special humidity requirement is noted; provide normal airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly in active growth if container growth is weak; avoid overfeeding.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: NC State recommends light shaping after flowering and removing winter-damaged wood after cold weather. Wear gloves; collect and dispose of all clippings safely because every part is poisonous.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists seed and stem cuttings for Nerium oleander. Handle cuttings with gloves and contain all toxic sap and debris.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: Nerium oleander is highly poisonous in every listed plant part, fresh or dry. NC State identifies cardiac glycosides and warns that ingestion can be fatal; smoke from burning prunings is injurious. Wear gloves, bag prunings, never burn them, and keep all parts away from children and animals.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Aphids, caterpillars, mealybugs and scale may occur, along with occasional leaf spot or sooty mold.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Prune dead or frost-damaged branches after winter; light pruning after flowering preserves next season’s buds. Never burn trimmings.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: NC State describes Lantana camara as a fast-growing, sprawling woody shrub with multicoloured flower clusters; in warm climates it may persist as a perennial.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Woody, often sprawling shrub with rough leaves and rounded clusters of small flowers in changing colour combinations.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Lantana camara prefers full sun, according to NC State Extension.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Lantana prefers moist but well-drained soil and tolerates drought after establishment.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: NC State recommends moist, well-drained soil for Lantana camara and notes tolerance of poorer soils and drought. Do not keep a container waterlogged.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Grow as a perennial in warm frost-free climates; in cooler conditions it may be treated as an annual.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm humid conditions are tolerated; allow airflow through the fast-growing shrub.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use light feeding only; excess fertilizer may reduce flowering.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Trim sprawling growth to contain it; remove spent growth as needed.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists seed, division and stem cuttings for Lantana camara. The source does not establish cultivar fidelity; retain cultivar-specific propagation details for review.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports whiteflies and spider mites on lantana kept indoors over winter; it also notes invasive behavior in some tropical regions. Inspect plants and contain berries where spread is a concern.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give sun and free drainage; control spreading and wear gloves if handling leaves or unripe berries.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Jatropha integerrima (peregrina/firecracker jatropha) is a tropical evergreen shrub or small tree native to Cuba and the West Indies. UF/IFAS reports multi-trunked growth, red or pink flowers through much of the year, and a landscape height and spread that can reach about 15 ft.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Jatropha integerrima has alternate leaves that may be oblong, fiddle-shaped or shallowly lobed, upright clusters of red or pink flowers, and capsules containing smooth, speckled seeds. Do not use J. podagrica’s bottle-shaped stem description for this taxon.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow Jatropha integerrima in full sun to partial shade; UF/IFAS notes that full sun promotes the best flowering.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Jatropha integerrima tolerates drought once established. NParks describes it as a little-water plant; use a freely draining container mix and avoid keeping the root zone saturated.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use well-drained soil for Jatropha integerrima. UF/IFAS lists tolerance of clay, sand or loam, but does not recommend waterlogged conditions.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep frost-free in a warm tropical position; avoid chilling a container plant.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Normal tropical humidity is acceptable; maintain airflow and avoid waterlogged roots.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use a light balanced feed during active growth; no exact rate is specified by UF/IFAS or NParks.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: UF/IFAS says Jatropha integerrima tolerates pruning and recommends pruning to develop strong structure. Its milky sap can irritate skin; wear gloves and avoid eye contact.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: UF/IFAS lists seed and cuttings as propagation methods for Jatropha integerrima. The seeds are toxic, so keep capsules and seed away from children and pets.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NParks identifies curcin and warns that all parts of Jatropha integerrima are poisonous if ingested; its milky sap may irritate skin. Keep the plant, capsules and seeds away from children and pets, and wear gloves when pruning.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: UF/IFAS reports occasional mites, scale and superficial leaf miner on Jatropha integerrima. Inspect before treating.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, shelter from prolonged monsoon saturation and reduce watering in cooler periods; established plants tolerate drought.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Canna indica is a tropical rhizomatous perennial with broad waxy leaves and red to yellow-orange flowers. It prefers sun and moist but well-drained soil; division and seed are propagation options.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Identify Canna indica by upright stems, broad sheathing leaves and terminal flower spikes; flowers range red to yellow-orange.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Canna indica prefers sunlight; partial shade is tolerated.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep soil moist but well drained; this tropical species tolerates wet seasons better than waterlogged pots.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use moist, well-drained soil; a range of textures is tolerated.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A tropical/subtropical rhizome; protect containers from cool weather and dormancy stress.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Heat and humidity suit Canna indica; good drainage remains important.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use balanced feed during active foliage and flowering growth; no species-specific dose is supplied.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove spent flower heads for continued flowering; cut back after the growing season only if foliage dies back.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide rhizomes or sow seed.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for canna rust, yellow mottle/streak viruses, leaf rollers, Japanese beetles and aphids.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Let leaves finish naturally after bloom; maintain free drainage during Dhaka’s rainy season.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Zephyranthes candida is a clumping bulbous perennial with narrow grass-like leaves and white crocus-like flowers, often appearing after rain. It grows in sun or partial shade and can be propagated by offsets.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: The species has narrow bright-green linear leaves and solitary silvery-white flowers with orange stamens.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Full sun gives best performance; partial shade is tolerated. Protect from extreme afternoon heat.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep soil moist in active growth; container bulbs need less water while dormant.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use freely draining soil that can retain some moisture.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: In cool climates bulbs are lifted before frost; in Dhaka keep them warm and sheltered from waterlogging.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: No special humidity is needed; focus on sun exposure and well-drained soil.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly while leaves are actively growing; allow foliage to mature after flowering.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove faded flowers at the base if you want to limit reseeding; keep green foliage until it yellows.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Separate offsets in spring; seed may also be collected.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Few serious problems are listed; inspect for slugs, snails and spider mites.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Let leaves finish naturally after bloom; maintain free drainage during Dhaka’s rainy season.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Hymenocallis littoralis is a tropical bulbous perennial with strap-shaped leaves and fragrant white spider-like flowers. The linked NC State page is genus-level and notes that species differ in habitat and hardiness.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Hymenocallis flowers have six narrow segments around a fused central cup, rising above basal strap leaves. Confirm H. littoralis from the bulb or plant label.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: The genus guide recommends full sun to partial shade; protect a container from extreme afternoon heat.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep actively growing bulbs moist but drain containers well; Hymenocallis species differ in wet-site tolerance.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use organic-rich soil with good drainage; the genus includes both wetland and drier-site species.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Most Hymenocallis need tropical or greenhouse warmth; protect bulbs from chilling.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm humid conditions suit tropical Hymenocallis; keep air moving around wet-season foliage.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly while leaves grow; stop feeding if the bulb becomes dormant.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove spent flower stalks and dead leaves; leave healthy leaves to replenish the bulb.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Separate offsets after flowering or during dormancy, keeping the basal plate intact.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State reports low-severity poison characteristics for Hymenocallis; bulbs may cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhea due to lycorine and related alkaloids. This is genus-level evidence; keep bulbs away from children and pets.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: The genus account notes occasional snails, caterpillars and mealybugs; monitor rather than treating preemptively.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, keep bulbs warm, provide drainage during monsoon rain and reduce watering only if foliage naturally goes dormant.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Impatiens balsamina is a frost-tender, fast-growing annual with succulent stems and cup-shaped flowers. It prefers moist conditions and readily self-seeds.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Garden balsam has succulent upright stems, serrated lance-shaped leaves and cup-shaped flowers; mature seed pods burst when touched.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow in full sun to partial shade.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep soil moist; garden balsam has low drought tolerance.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: It tolerates varied soil textures and pH; choose a moist, well-drained mix.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A frost-tender annual; grow in warm weather.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: No special humidity treatment is noted; avoid stagnant crowded growth.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use moderate fertility; no exact dose is supplied by the source.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove spent growth if you want to limit self-seeding; handle ripe pods gently because they burst.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Grow from seed; ripe pods can eject seed when touched.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: The plant self-seeds readily and can spread; large raw leaf quantities may pose low-severity oxalate risk.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give morning sun and afternoon shade in peak heat; protect pots from monsoon waterlogging.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Impatiens walleriana is a compact, mounding tropical perennial often grown as a bedding annual. It flowers in shade to part shade and prefers moist, well-drained soil.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Common impatiens has succulent branching stems, oval serrated leaves and conspicuously spurred flowers; cultivars vary.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Part shade to full shade is best; too much sun can scorch leaves.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep moist but well drained; hot, dry spells need extra water, while overwatering can cause rot.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use moist, well-drained soil supplemented with organic material and slightly acidic pH.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A tropical perennial, but cold-tender; protect from cold weather.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: It tolerates humidity, but heat and dry spells can cause wilting.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use modest balanced feeding in active growth; no exact rate is stated.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Trim back about one-third when plants become leggy in late summer.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Use seed or cuttings; take cuttings in fall and plant out after cold weather passes.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Check for aphids, nematodes, spider mites, slugs, snails, powdery/downy mildew and wilt.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give morning sun and afternoon shade in peak heat; protect pots from monsoon waterlogging.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Impatiens hawkeri (New Guinea impatiens) is a tropical mounding bedding plant with glossy foliage and colorful flowers; NC State notes partial shade and moist, organic, well-drained soil.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Impatiens hawkeri is sold in many New Guinea impatiens cultivars; glossy leaves and showy flowers are common, but exact shape and color depend on cultivar. The catalog does not record a cultivar name.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Partial shade is best, but Impatiens hawkeri tolerates a wider light range than common impatiens.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the soil moist and well drained; more sun means more water.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use moist, organic-rich, well-drained soil.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: A warm-season plant; grow in frost-free conditions.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Warm humid conditions suit this tropical impatiens; provide airflow in wet weather.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly during active flowering growth; no specific dose is provided.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Pinch or trim leggy stems to keep the mound compact; remove damaged foliage.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Sow seed in warm soil (70–75°F); cuttings are also commonly used for named cultivars.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State describes resistance to downy mildew and no serious insect issues; monitor for leaf spot and root rot.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, give morning sun and afternoon shade in peak heat; protect pots from monsoon waterlogging.
